In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of anoxic injury in white matter.
the role of Na+ influx in the pathogenesis of anoxic injury in myelinating white matter.
the role of Ca2+ in the pathogenesis of anoxic injury to myelinated axon within the CNS, and the coupling between Na(+)-dependent Ca2+ entry, and Ca(2+) -mediated injury.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
anoxia causes a massive influx of Na+ into axons, which in turn triggers a Ca2+-mediating injury.
TTX prevents Na+ influx and thus the resulting rise in intracellular Na+, which in turn prevents Ca2+ entry via the Na(+)/Ca(2+) exchanger.

the ultrastructural changes seen in anoxic injury are due to the influx of Na+ and the resultant increase in intracellular Ca2+ concentration, which leads to the activation of a number of Ca2+-dependent enzymes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

anoxic injury of rat CNS white matter is characterized by a rapid and severe loss of function which is associated with ultrastructural changes consistent with the hypothesis that the loss of function is due to depolariation and run-down of transmembrane Na gradients.
the anoxic injury of the optic nerve is a good model to study the pathophysiology of ischemia and that the TTX treatment can be used to study the role of Na+ influx in ischemia.
TTX prevents the loss of axonal cytoskeletal proteins and the appearance of submyelinic spaces, but not the mitochondrial changes, in the anoxic CNS.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the axon is the most susceptible component of the optic nerve.
the ultrastructural effects on axons and myelinating glia in anoxic white matter are dependent upon Na+ influx.
the ultrastructural changes seen in anoxic optic axons are prevented by blocking Na+ influx with tetrodotoxine.
